newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss lower house approves central bank law change.
newsitem.headline: Swiss lower house approves central bank law change.

text.p: Switzerland's lower house of parliament approved on Thursday proposed changes to the Swiss National Bank's (SNB) legal charter which would give the central bank greater freedom in managing its reserves.
The SNB hopes to generate 400 million Swiss francs in additional income from better management of assets. Two-thirds would go to Swiss cantons and one third to the federal government.
The revision is unrelated to a planned revaluation of the SNB's gold reserves, which would finance a humanitarian fund for victims of poverty and disasters in Switzerland and abroad.

The proposals, based on a report by the SNB and finance ministry officials, would allow the central bank to use derivatives and invest in longer-dated and higher yielding debt of foreign states, banks or international organisations.
One of the main attractions of the revision is that it would allow the central bank to invest currency reserves in instruments with maturities of more than one year.

The measure now moves to the upper house, where approval is expected. Assuming there is no great opposition to the plan, the revised laws could be in force by the end of the year, an SNB spokesman has said.

These proposals are unrelated to the plan to use official gold reserves held by the SNB to create a seven billion Swiss franc humanitarian fund. The plan, which must still be approved by Swiss voters next year, would entail selling gold over a 10-year period.
The federal government and the Swiss cantons, the principal owners of the central bank, are entitled to the proceeds from SNB's currency investments.
A parliamentarian who had proposed using some these profits to stock up the planned humanitarian fund withdrew his motion. -- Zurich Editorial +41 1 631 7340
